content.title: About
content.content: Breading and batter are mixtures used to coat foods before frying, baking, or boiling. Breading typically consists of breadcrumbs, flour, spices, and sometimes cheese, while batter may include flour, eggs, milk, water, and leavening agents. They give dishes a crisp crust, lock in moisture, and enhance flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Breaded dishes date back to ancient Rome, where crushed bread was used to fry fish.
Tempura batter is a Japanese specialty made with cold water and flour, without eggs.
Gluten‑free breadings often use rice flour, cornflakes, or nut meals.
Seasoned breadcrumbs can be flavored with herbs, parmesan, or smoked paprika.
A classic French batters for frying (à la friteuse) uses a 1:1.5‑2 flour‑to‑liquid ratio.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: A thin batter layer slows carbohydrate absorption, helping to avoid sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Increased satiety
items.content: Breading that contains protein (egg, cheese) and fiber (whole‑grain flour) can keep you fuller longer.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Flour and eggs provide thiamine, riboflavin, and pyridoxine, which support metabolism.

items.title: Mineral contribution
items.content: Whole‑grain breadcrumbs supply iron, magnesium, and zinc.

items.title: Antioxidant boost
items.content: Adding spices such as paprika or turmeric to breading raises antioxidant content.

items.title: High calorie load
items.content: Breading and batter add fat and carbs, making dishes calorie‑dense.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional wheat‑based breading is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Trans‑fat formation during frying
items.content: Using highly refined oils at high temperatures can generate trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Pre‑made breadcrumb mixes often contain added salt; those with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Dredge meat, fish, or vegetables in flour, dip in beaten egg, then coat with breadcrumbs; fry until golden. For batter, whisk flour, eggs, and liquid, dip the food, and deep‑fry or pan‑fry. Batter can also be used to bake vegetables, fish, or make fritters.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry breading mixes in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 6 months. Fresh batter should be used immediately, but can be refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Store away from strong odors, as breadcrumbs absorb them.

content.title: About
content.content: A burrito bowl with beans is a nutritious bowl that combines rice or quinoa, black or red beans, fresh vegetables, salsa, guacamole, and seasonings. The dish captures Mexican flavors in a convenient, tortilla‑free format, making it easy to eat and suitable for vegetarians.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The burrito bowl gained popularity in the United States in the early 2010s as a healthier alternative to traditional burritos.
Beans are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, grown for more than 7,000 years.
Traditional recipes often use black beans, which are rich in antioxidants.
The bowl can be customized for various diets by adding chicken, tofu, or swapping rice for cauliflower rice.
Salsa, a key component, can range from mild to spicy depending on the tomatoes and spices used.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 15 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice or quinoa offers sustained energy release, beneficial for active individuals.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The bowl supplies vitamin C, potassium, magnesium, and iron, especially when topped with fresh veggies and guacamole.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Most fats come from avocado and olive oil, which are heart‑healthy.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: High sodium in sauces
items.content: Store‑bought salsas often contain a lot of salt; choose low‑sodium versions or make them at home.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gas in sensitive individuals; proper soaking and cooking reduce this effect.

items.title: Calorie density with added cheese or sour cream
items.content: Large amounts of cheese, sour cream, or mayo can significantly increase the bowl’s calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the bowl in a deep plate or bowl. Mix all ingredients together, then add lime juice, fresh cilantro, or hot sauce to taste. It can be enjoyed warm or cold.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared bowl in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Store sauces separately to prevent soggy vegetables. When reheating, use a microwave or skillet with a splash of water to avoid drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken fillet wrap sandwich, fried is a fast‑food item consisting of a breaded chicken fillet wrapped in a thin tortilla and deep‑fried. The sandwich combines a crispy exterior, juicy meat and fresh vegetables, often served with a sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish appeared in the early 2000s as a lighter fast‑food alternative.
The chicken fillet is usually marinated in spices and breaded before frying.
The wrap can be made from wheat, whole‑grain or gluten‑free flour.
Some locations add avocado or cheddar cheese for extra flavor.
It is commonly served with french fries and a soft drink.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken fillet provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Lower fat than beef
items.content: Chicken contains less saturated fat than red meat, making it a more heart‑friendly option.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The wrap’s carbohydrates give a quick boost of energy.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sauces and seasonings can raise the salt level, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Trans fats in breading
items.content: Deep‑frying can create trans fats that are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich can be high in calories due to oil and bread, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is hand‑held; you can add fresh lettuce, tomatoes or extra sauce to taste. For a lighter version, choose a whole‑grain wrap and limit the amount of sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, keep the components separate and assemble just before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee, cafe con leche is a hot beverage made from espresso, steamed milk, and a touch of sugar. It is popular in Latin American countries and is often served in cafés as a light breakfast or afternoon drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “café con leche” comes from Spanish and literally means “coffee with milk”.
In Spain and Latin America the drink is usually served in large ceramic cups.
Adding milk mellows the bitterness of coffee, making it more approachable for children.
Some regions use whole milk, others opt for skimmed or plant‑based milks (soy, almond, etc.).
Coffee, as we know it, became popular in Europe in the 19th century after being exported from the colonies.

items.title: Energizing effect
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving alertness and reducing fatigue.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals and may lower the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine can boost metabolic rate and aid in calorie burning.

items.title: Calcium from milk
items.content: The milk component provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee contains small amounts of vitamins B2 and B3, which play roles in energy metabolism.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine consumption.

items.title: Increased acidity
items.content: Coffee can aggravate acid reflux in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The milk in the drink may cause discomfort for those who cannot digest lactose.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Sugar raises the calorie count and can contribute to dental caries.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot immediately after preparation. Optionally sprinkle cinnamon or add a dash of vanilla for extra aroma. For a vegan version, replace dairy milk with soy, oat, or almond milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ground coffee in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, and keep milk refrigerated and use within 5 days. Use fresh ingredients each time you prepare the drink.

content.title: About
content.content: Ritz cheese‑filled sandwich crackers are crisp bite‑size squares topped with a smooth creamy cheese spread. They are convenient for snacking, suitable for kids’ lunches, and often used as a base for appetizers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product is marketed under the Ritz brand, owned by Mondelez International.
The cheese filling is made from pasteurized milk and cream cheese, giving it a soft texture.
Crackers are shaped as small squares, ideal for portioned packaging.
A modest amount of salt and vegetable oil is added to enhance flavor.
They are frequently included in school lunch boxes and children’s snack packs.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese filling provides calcium, which supports bone and teeth health.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Carbohydrates in the crackers are rapidly digested, giving a fast energy boost.

items.title: Contains vitamin A
items.content: Cream cheese contributes small amounts of vitamin A, beneficial for vision.

items.title: Convenient snack
items.content: Portion‑controlled packs help manage calorie intake.

items.title: Balanced snack option
items.content: The mix of carbs and a modest amount of fat makes it a relatively balanced light snack.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The cheese filling may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy allergies.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: People monitoring salt intake, such as those with hypertension, should consume in moderation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although the serving size is small, the product contains a notable amount of calories, so consider overall daily intake.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Some versions may contain partially hydrogenated oils; check the ingredient list.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the crackers straight from the pack, use them as a base for canapés, crumble them into salads, or pair with fruit dips. Their compact size makes them easy to carry in a bag or backpack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place, tightly sealed. For extended freshness, keep the package refrigerated to maintain crispness and prevent rancidity.

content.title: About
content.content: Mushrooms are edible fruiting bodies of fungi that are widely used in cooking. Cooked mushrooms (NS) are a ready‑to‑eat product obtained by heat treatment, preserving most nutrients and their characteristic aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushrooms belong to a separate kingdom of living organisms – the fungal kingdom.
Cooked mushrooms are a staple in Asian cuisine, especially in soups and stews.
Mushrooms can accumulate vitamin D when exposed to ultraviolet light.
There are over 10,000 edible mushroom species, but commercially cultivated button mushrooms and oyster mushrooms dominate the market.
Mushrooms can be grown in controlled environments, making them available year‑round.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cooked mushrooms provide about 3 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A cup of cooked mushrooms (≈100 g) contains only about 22 kcal, suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms contain niacin, riboflavin, and vitamin B6, which are essential for metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Cooked mushrooms provide selenium, potassium, and copper, supporting immune function and nervous system health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The fiber in mushrooms aids digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms, manifested as skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Mushrooms contain chitin, which in large amounts can cause discomfort for people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial or mold growth; only consume fresh or properly preserved mushrooms.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Mushrooms are relatively high in purines, so people with gout should limit their intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked mushrooms can be added to soups, sauces, salads, pasta, and omelets. They are also used as a topping for pies and pizza. For extra flavor, briefly sauté them before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked mushrooms in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Discard any mushrooms with off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Green pickled tomatoes are young tomato fruits harvested before full ripening and brined in a mixture of vinegar, salt, and spices. They have a crisp texture, a mildly sour and aromatic flavor, and a vivid green color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled green tomatoes are popular in Mediterranean, Eastern European, and American cuisines.
Traditional recipes include vinegar, garlic, dill, mustard seeds, and pepper.
In some regions they are called “tomato cornichons” because of their similarity to pickled cucumbers.
Green tomatoes are rich in antioxidants such as lutein and beta‑carotene, which are retained during pickling.
During the Soviet era they were commonly served as a side dish with sauerkraut.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant that may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup of pickled tomatoes contains about 30 kcal, making them a suitable snack for weight control.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Acidity and fiber promote gastric juice production and intestinal motility.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: They supply potassium, magnesium, and iron, essential for normal body functions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Excess salt can raise blood pressure; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic brine may irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes, manifested as skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial versions may contain additives such as sulfites, which can cause sensitivity in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled green tomatoes are enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, pastas, stews, and fermented dishes. Slice them into rounds or use whole fruits to garnish plates.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the jar refrigerated after opening. Properly stored, they retain flavor and texture for 2–3 weeks. Discard if the brine becomes cloudy, develops an off‑odor, or the tomatoes become soft.
